main.t: The lower jaw: the only skull bone that moves (mandible).

simpler.t: The mandible is your lower jaw bone.

deeper.t: It is one of two unpaired facial bones; the other is the vomer.

facts.t: It forms the lower jaw, below the upper jaw bones (maxillae).
At the back, each side rises to meet the temporal bone just in front of the ear canal.
The hyoid bone lies just below it, in the upper neck.

simpler.t: It forms your chin and lower jaw, and hinges just in front of your ears.

deeper.t: Each condyle sits in the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone, with a disc between them.

items.name: Body
items.t: The horizontal, U-shaped part that holds the lower teeth.

items.name: Ramus
items.t: The upright part at the back of each side (“ramus” means branch).

items.name: Angle
items.t: The corner where the body and ramus meet.

items.name: Condylar process
items.t: The back projection, topped by the condyle. It forms the jaw joint with the temporal bone.

items.name: Coronoid process
items.t: The flat front projection. A biting muscle attaches to it.

items.name: Mandibular foramen
items.t: An opening on the inner ramus. The nerve and vessels to the lower teeth enter here.

items.name: Mental foramen
items.t: An opening at the front. A sensory nerve to the chin comes out here.

items.name: Alveolar process
items.t: The top edge of the body, which anchors the lower teeth.

items.name: Mylohyoid line
items.t: A ridge inside the body. The muscle forming the floor of the mouth attaches here.

simpler.t: It has a curved body for the teeth and two upright parts that reach up to the skull.

deeper.t: The condylar process forms the jaw joint; the coronoid process anchors a biting muscle.

facts.t: As the mouth opens, the jaw hinges down and the condyle glides forwards onto a bony bump (articular tubercle). This lets the mouth open wide.
A flexible disc between the condyle and the temporal bone smooths the movement.
Its processes and ridges give attachment to the strong chewing muscles.

simpler.t: It hinges and slides at the jaw joint, so you can open wide and chew.

items.name: Temporomandibular joint
items.t: The condyle meets the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone.

items.name: Chewing muscles
items.t: Arise from the zygomatic arch and fill the temporal and infratemporal fossae. They move the mandible.

items.name: Trigeminal nerve
items.t: Controls the chewing muscles and gives feeling to the face.

items.name: Inferior alveolar nerve
items.t: The nerve to the lower teeth: enters the mandibular foramen.
items.check: OpenStax describes the nerve without naming it; “inferior alveolar nerve” needs an approved source.

items.name: Ligament to the lingula
items.t: From the base of the skull to the lingula. It steadies the jaw as the mouth opens and closes.

items.name: Floor of the mouth
items.t: The muscle forming the floor of the mouth attaches to the mylohyoid lines.

simpler.t: Chewing muscles move it, and nerves to the lower teeth and chin run through it.

facts.t: At birth, it is in two halves. They fuse during the first year into one U-shaped bone.
In childhood the jaws grow as the teeth come in. This enlarges the face.
Like other flat bones of the face, most of it forms directly from membrane (intramembranous ossification).
facts.check: OpenStax says the flat bones of the face develop this way; that this includes most of the mandible needs an approved source.

facts.t: In males the angle of the mandible tends to be squarer and more flared.

items.injury: Opening the mouth too wide, as in a large bite, or a blow to the jaw.
items.damaged: The jaw joint dislocates: the condyle moves in front of the articular tubercle.
items.why: The condyle is stuck in front of the tubercle and cannot slide back.

items.injury: A dental injection near the mandibular foramen.
items.damaged: The sensory nerve to the lower teeth.
items.cannotDo: Feel the lower teeth on that side.
items.why: The nerve is reached before it enters the foramen and runs through the bone to the teeth.

items.injury: Arthritis, grinding of the teeth or damage to the disc (temporomandibular joint disorder).
items.damaged: The jaw joint and its disc.
items.cannotDo: Chew comfortably; sometimes move the jaw at all (“lock jaw”).
items.why: The worn or damaged joint surfaces no longer glide smoothly.

items.q: Explain how the temporomandibular joint lets the mouth open wide.
model: At the same time the condyle and disc glide forwards onto the articular tubercle.
The net movement of the condyle is forwards and downwards.
The disc smooths the movement between the bones.

items.q: A patient yawns widely and cannot close their mouth. Predict where the condyle is.
model: The condyle has moved forwards, in front of the articular tubercle.
It cannot slide back into the mandibular fossa.

items.q: Compare the mandibular foramen and the mental foramen.
model: Mandibular foramen: on the inner side of the ramus.
The nerve and vessels to the lower teeth enter it.
Mental foramen: at the front of the body, on each side.
A sensory nerve to the chin comes out through it.

check.stem: Which bone of the skull can move?
check.why: The mandible is the only skull bone that moves.

check.stem: Which part of the mandible forms the temporomandibular joint?
check.why: The condyle meets the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone.

check.stem: To numb the lower teeth, where must a dentist inject?
options: Where the nerve enters the mandibular foramen
check.why: The nerve to the lower teeth must be reached before it enters the mandibular foramen.
